note: Bytes are served verbatim by _build/harness/harness.py and must be captured verbatim.
Four of these payloads are gzip. Do not decompress before saving, do not open them in an
editor, and do not let a capture script call .decode() on the way to disk. The entire point
of this fixture set is that the raw bytes are what a validator sees, and a helpful
decompression anywhere in the capture path destroys the only thing being tested.
Wayback needs a 120 second timeout with backoff. It fails at 30 seconds.
CDX routes match on two order-independent lookaheads: the target url AND the from= anchor.
Requiring the anchor in the pattern is deliberate. An unanchored CDX query matches no route and
raises FixtureMiss naming the url, so a contract that forgets to anchor fails the offline suite
immediately instead of passing against a body whose rows it could not have received. Snapshot
routes match exactly, because the /web/<timestamp>id_/<url> shape is fixed and an inexact
timestamp must stay detectable.
Captured live 2026-08-25. Two things the capture pass measured that this manifest did not
predict, both recorded per route below as captured_* keys rather than by editing the original
claims, so the drift stays visible:
1. RESOLVED 2026-08-25, same day. expect.contains_timestamp failed on four of the five original
CDX routes, and the cause was limit=, not a missing capture. CDX returns matching rows oldest
first, so a bounded limit= over a wide window returns the EARLIEST N change points and a
recent pin falls off the end. Measured: aws-terms over from=20260101&to=20260901&limit=40
returned 40 rows without the pin, and the same query narrowed to from=20260801 returned 6
rows WITH it. The one route whose pins were present, cdx-gcp-deprecation, was the one route
returning fewer rows (5) than its limit. The pinned snapshots themselves all existed and all
replayed fine, so this was a query-window defect and not archive drift.
The fix needs no new parameter: anchor from= at the timestamp the call depends on. Verified
live by _scan/check-cdx-window-anchoring.py that from=<full 14-digit timestamp> INCLUDES the
row at that instant and places it at index 0, and that it stays at index 0 at limit=5. All
six routes were then recaptured by _scan/recapture-cdx-anchored.py with from=<pin>&to=<now>
&limit=200, and 6 of 6 now hold every pin with the anchor at row 0. Two saturate the limit,
which is safe rather than broken, because truncation now lands only on change points later
than anything the anchored call depends on.
Two consequences worth carrying into the contract. First, openai-tou is now TWO routes: its
pins are 27 months apart with more than 200 distinct digests between them, so one window
cannot hold both, and a bond anchors at its own baseline rather than at a range covering
every baseline anyone might pick. Second, cloud.google.com/terms produces roughly 2.5 change
points a day, so a check must advance its cursor to the newest row it EXAMINED and never to
the wall clock, or the rows past the ceiling become a silent skip.
2. Three snapshot routes answer 302 at the url spelled here and 200 one path-normalisation
away. In all three the Location carries a byte-identical 14-digit timestamp and differs
only by a trailing slash, so it is Wayback normalising a URL and not Wayback substituting
the nearest snapshot. The bytes were taken from the normalised URL, recorded as
captured_url, and the pinned url is deliberately left as-is: it is the harness match key,
and a 302 on the unslashed form is itself part of what this project tests.

capture.example_note: Generated by the contract's own cdx_query_url, not hand-written. It differs from capture.query in two parameters and both are correct: the capture sent fl=timestamp,digest,length,statuscode and limit=200 to measure how many change points these pages really have, while the contract sends fl=timestamp,digest,length and the limit its caller passed. capture.query is provenance for the bytes; example is what routing must match.

expect.note: This route was named 'snap-gcp-deprecation-incomplete' and declared gate REJECTED with a blank frame, on the theory that it was a truncated capture caught by the terminal marker gate. That was asserted without being measured and it is false. Measured 2026-08-25 by _scan/check-holdfast-gates.py: the gzip stream is complete, it decodes to 696794 bytes, and the document ends '...</devsite-a11y-announce>\n  </body>\n</html>', which is identical in shape to the tail of the qualified GCP terms capture. Its real value is that it is the fifth 1f8b payload in the set, and without it the 'a build that skips decompression fails five of nine' claim in 06-holdfast.md section 11 is only four. No anchor, sections or terminal are declared for this page anywhere, so no gate can be evaluated on it and none is claimed. The negative gate case is snap-github-tos-chrome-only, which is synthetic and labelled so.

routes.name: snap-github-tos-chrome-only
routes.note: SYNTHETIC, DERIVED. Not a live capture, and the url above is not a real archive url: it carries a ?shell=1 marker so it can never be mistaken for one or accidentally re-fetched. Every payload actually captured for this project qualifies once decoded, proven by _scan/prove-gate-measurement-bug.py, so gates B, C and D had no negative fixture at all. A gate with no negative fixture is untested code guarding a payout, so this one is derived by a rule stated in advance: take the real GitHub ToS capture and delete the span from its first section heading to its last, keeping head, nav and footer, which is the shape an unhydrated single-page shell has. Nothing is inserted and no string is hand-authored. GitHub was chosen because it is the only one of the four pages whose declared gate inputs are mutually independent; on aws and gcp the declared terminal marker is a substring of the anchor or of a section word, so gate D there cannot fail on its own.

expect.note: Gate B passing here is the measurement worth having, not a defect: a shell carries the page title, so B cannot catch it and C and D must. That is the first evidence in this project that B, C and D do separate work rather than being one gate wearing three names. It decodes cleanly and closes with </html>, so no decoder catches it and only the gate can. The interface must render a blank frame that cannot be confused with an unchanged frame.

CDX length understates the payload by 7.84x, which is why length cannot pre-flight a size gate. Exercises all three caps. Served identity, not gzip: magic 3c21, and raw equals decoded, so like snap-openai-tou-identity it never enters the decode branch. Its 35689 extracted chars are the inflated half of the gate A pair recorded in 06-holdfast.md section 2 against 2738 chars for the same page with no policy change, which is the surviving measured reason gate A is disabled by default.

routes.name: cdx-never-archived

capture.example_note: The target is synthetic and deliberately unresolvable. What is real is the response: Wayback answers a URL it has never archived with HTTP 200 and three bytes, and no part of that is an error the contract can detect from the status line.

routes.note: The most dangerous response in the data path: 200 with a 3-byte body, not a 404. Served inline rather than from a file so it cannot be accidentally edited into something plausible.
